top_stories.title: Apple builds its own China-specific AI model with Alibaba's help
points: Apple trained an in-house large language model (LLM — an AI system trained on text to generate and understand language) specifically for China, with technical assistance from Alibaba.
Previously, every AI feature on iPhones in China ran on external models owned by other companies.
Beijing registered/approved Apple's generative AI service last month, clearing regulatory hurdles for an Apple Intelligence launch in China within months.
The shift gives Apple control over user data flows and aligns with China's data localization rules.

unique_angles.point: Frames it as Apple's broader strategy of building localized AI capabilities in key markets rather than relying solely on local partners.
Presents it as a template for how big tech builds region-specific AI infrastructure to comply with local regulation.

top_stories.title: Speed wars: Gemini 3.7 Flash price cut vs. OpenAI's Ultrafast mode
points: Google released Gemini 3.7 Flash at 340 tokens per second (tokens = word fragments a model reads/writes), about 2x faster than GPT-5.6 Luna, and halved the prior price.
Gemini 3.7 Flash remains 8x more expensive than ultra-cheap options like GPT-5.6 Luna, leaving it in an awkward middle on cost-per-intelligence.
OpenAI countered with Ultrafast mode for GPT-5.6 Sol at 750 tokens/second — 14x normal speed — running on specialized Cerebras hardware.
Ultrafast targets latency-sensitive workflows such as real-time voice and customer support, previously ruled out by delay.
Anthropic's Claude can now work directly inside browser tabs with full channel context, removing copy-paste between apps.

unique_angles.point: Vercel engineers call Gemini 3.7 Flash "on the Pareto frontier" (best available tradeoff between competing factors) and a daily driver for interactive coding.
Argues the model race is fragmenting into parallel competitions over distribution, harnesses, revenue and speed — not just raw intelligence.
Groups the week's upgrades across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok as a broad reshaping of AI economics.

top_stories.title: ChatGPT Computer History shifts AI's bottleneck to context
points: ChatGPT's Computer History on macOS logs typing, clicks and app switches — not screenshots — so the assistant learns how a specific person actually works.
Approach is explicitly less privacy-invasive than screenshot-based tools like Windows Recall.
Paired with Grok Bot's "Teach a Task" (record a browser workflow once, AI replays it on a schedule or trigger), it suggests models are capable enough and the blocker is knowing a user's workflow.

unique_angles.point: Early Grok Bot users: a plumbing company owner automated dispatch and office tasks in 24 hours with no engineers, while power users hit limits like no folder-targeting and no model choice.

items.title: Meta assembling a large coding dataset
points: Meta is building a comprehensive coding dataset to address scarcity of high-quality training data for code-generating models.
Coding data underpins models that write, debug and optimize software, making the asset strategically valuable.
Signals intensifying competition in AI-assisted software development.

items.title: Google's multi-embodiment robot learning
points: Google trains a single robot model across multiple robot body types at once instead of one model per robot.
Multi-embodiment training (exposing a model to diverse physical forms and movement patterns) yields skills that transfer between machines.
Targets a core robotics limitation: models trained on one hardware design rarely work on another.

items.title: MiniMax's "open" video model carries commercial restrictions
points: MiniMax released an open video generation model pitched as democratizing video AI.
License restricts commercial use, so companies can't build products on it without separate licensing.
An "open with an asterisk" release: public code, legal limits on real-world use.

items.title: OpenAI nears $40B annualized revenue run rate
points: Annualized revenue passed $40 billion per Bloomberg, roughly doubling from late 2025.
Run rate grew more than 20% in July alone, driven by ChatGPT subscriptions, Codex (its code-generation tool) and advertising.
Momentum sets the stage for OpenAI's planned IPO.

items.title: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 gains come purely from post-training
points: Terminal-Bench 3.0 coding score jumped from 4.6% to 28.3%; CyberGym security benchmark hit 84.5%.
Base model size unchanged at 743 billion parameters — all gains from one extra month of post-training (extra tuning after the main training run).
Weights still pending safety checks and all results are vendor-reported, not independently verified.

items.title: Microsoft retires four Copilot features on August 18
points: Group chats and Labs are among the four features being cut.
Copilot consolidates into a single work/personal app, dropping the Mico mascot.

items.title: Gemini's visible watermark can be toggled off
points: One setting flip removes the visible watermark from all images, video and audio generated afterward.
The invisible SynthID tag (a unique fingerprint embedded in the file) stays, proving AI generation to systems that check.
C2PA metadata (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity provenance standard) also remains attached.

items.title: Six AI myths fact-checked
points: Water per ChatGPT prompt is ~15 milliliters, not a full bottle — the original claim's author revised it down.
Radiologist displacement never happened; the field faces a shortage with salaries above $570,000.
Air-conditioning load on the grid will exceed all AI systems on Earth combined.
Hallucination rate (confidently false answers) fell from ~20% to under 1% as models scaled.
Progress passed an "invisibility threshold" where gains kept compounding but stopped being obvious to humans.
Myths persist because they answer emotional questions; two questions defuse them — what exactly broke, and what's the source?

items.title: OpenAI builder's guide: let smaller models think longer
points: Guide shows startups cutting costs by giving smaller models more reasoning time instead of upgrading to bigger ones.
Recommendations are backed by benchmark data.

items.title: Anthropic peer-review experiment with 45 AI agents
points: Red team gave 45 AI agents their own isolated machines to operate independently.
Agents peer-reviewed each other's work to surface failures and unsafe behavior.
Goal: measure what breaks under self-scrutiny and whether agent teams catch errors internal review misses.

items.title: Cheap Chinese models don't actually save money
points: AlphaSense study on financial-analysis tasks found GPT-5.6 Sol was 13% cheaper and 20% higher quality than Kimi K3.
Pricier models use tokens more efficiently, so cost-per-task completed beats sticker price per token as a buying metric.
Undercuts the narrative that Chinese model commoditization will win on price alone.

items.title: OpenAI's Chief Revenue Officer departs
points: Denise Dresser left after nine months, the second executive exit in a single week.
Turnover raises concerns ahead of a delayed IPO.

items.title: The AI Deputization Audit framework
points: Five-question scorecard rates each recurring task 0–2 on frequency/duration, teachability in a 10-minute screen share, output-checking speed, cost of errors, and person-specificity.
Scores of 8–10 mean "Deputize" (hand off fully), 4–7 "Duet" (AI does part), 0–3 "Defend" (keep it yourself).
Old blockers like no API for legacy software or hard-to-document workflows are now solvable via Computer History and Teach a Task.
Emerging practice: one bot per topic reporting to a single "chief of staff" bot, starting with inbox/Slack tracking plus a morning briefing.

points: 1. Visible watermark disappears with one setting flip on all images, video, and audio generated after activation.

3. C2PA data (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity standard metadata) stays attached, so files still disclose their AI origin to tools that read it.
4. Toggle is user-controlled—visible mark removal doesn't affect provenance tracking underneath.

headlines: Google released Gemini 3.7 Flash at 340 tokens per second (roughly 2x faster than GPT-5.6 Luna) and half the prior price, but still 8x more expensive than ultra-cheap options, creating a tradeoff between speed and cost that some developers find worth paying for.

OpenAI countered with Ultrafast mode for GPT-5.6 Sol running at 750 tokens per second (14x normal speed on specialized Cerebras hardware), targeting latency-sensitive workflows like real-time voice and customer support.

Study finds cheaper Chinese AI models (Kimi K3, GLM-5.2) don't actually save money in practice because higher-priced models use tokens more efficiently—GPT-5.6 Sol beat Kimi K3 on both cost and quality.
OpenAI's Chief Revenue Officer Denise Dresser departed after nine months, the second executive exit in one week, feeding concerns about turnover ahead of a delayed IPO.

ChatGPT's Computer History and Grok Bot's Teach a Task features shift AI's bottleneck from raw capability to contextual knowledge—users can now teach AI their specific workflows through interaction logs or screen recordings rather than descriptions.

sections.title: The Speed Wars Are Reshaping Model Competition
points: Gemini 3.7 Flash trades frontier performance for speed (340 tokens/second, 2x faster than GPT-5.6 Luna) and cut prices in half, but remains 8x more expensive than ultra-cheap alternatives like GPT-5.6 Luna, leaving it in an awkward middle position on the cost-per-intelligence tradeoff.

Vercel engineers report real wins in production for interactive coding work where speed justifies the premium, calling Gemini 3.7 Flash "on the Pareto frontier" (optimal balance between competing factors) as a daily driver.

OpenAI's Ultrafast mode pushes GPT-5.6 Sol to 750 tokens per second (14x normal speed) on specialized Cerebras hardware, positioning speed as its own competitive axis rather than chasing frontier performance.
The model race is fragmenting into parallel competitions around distribution, harnesses, revenue, and speed—not just raw intelligence—signaling a mature market segmenting by use case.

sections.title: Cost Per Task, Not Token Price, Determines True Savings
points: AlphaSense study of financial-analysis tasks found GPT-5.6 Sol beats Kimi K3 on both cost (13% cheaper) and quality (20% higher), despite Kimi K3's lower per-token price.
Higher-priced models end up cheaper overall because they use tokens more efficiently—meaning enterprise buyers must judge models on cost-per-task completed rather than sticker price per token.
This insight directly challenges the narrative that Chinese AI commoditization will undercut Western models purely on price.

sections.title: AI's Bottleneck Shifts from Capability to Context
points: ChatGPT's Computer History logs clicks, typing, and app switches (instead of screenshots like Windows Recall) so AI learns how a specific person actually works without privacy-invasive constant screenshots.
Grok Bot's Teach a Task feature lets users record a workflow once in the browser and AI repeats it as a scheduled or triggered routine—best deployed when the bot already struggles on its own.
Two new features signal that models are now capable enough; the real blocker is whether they know how a particular user works, not whether they can execute the task in theory.

Early Grok Bot deployments show a plumbing company owner went from zero automation to automated dispatch and office tasks in 24 hours without engineers, while power users hit constraints like no folder-targeting and no model choice.

sections.title: The AI Deputization Audit Framework
points: Five-question scorecard scores each recurring task 0–2 on frequency/duration, teachability in a 10-minute screen share, output-checking speed, cost of errors, and person-specificity.
Tasks scoring 8–10 are "Deputize" candidates (hand off entirely); 4–7 is "Duet" (AI handles part of work); 0–3 means "Defend" (keep it).

Framework then identifies what's actually blocking Duet or Defend tasks—many blockers that were dealbreakers (no API for legacy software, workflows hard to document but easy to show) are now solvable by Computer History and Teach a Task features.
Emerging best practice: spin up individual bots per topic reporting to a single "chief of staff" bot, paired with a common starter project like inbox/Slack tracking plus morning briefing.
